chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Khalid al-Kabuli, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

We found in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him): 'Surely the earth is Allah's; He causes such of His servants to inherit it as He so desires, and the end is for those who are pious.' I and the people of my Household are those who inherited the earth, and we are the pious, and the earth, all of it, is for us.
So whoever from the Muslims revives a land, let him develop it, and let him pay its taxes (kharaj) to the Imam from my Household, and for him is whatever he consumes from it.

So if he neglects it or ruins it, and another man from the Muslims takes it from after him, so he develops it and revives it, so he would be more rightful with it than the one who neglected it. So let him pay its taxes to the Imam from my Household, and for him is whatever he consumes.

Until the Appearance of Al-Qa'im (peace be upon him) from my family with the sword, so he would allow it and prevent it, and he would throw them out from it just as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) allowed it and prevented it.
Except whatever was in the hands of our Shiah, for he would cut it out for them upon what is in their hands and he would leave the land in their hands.
ai.seo_question: What are the rules for reviving and owning land in Shia jurisprudence according to the Imams?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi grounds the jurisprudence of *ihya al-mawat* (reviving dead lands) in the theological concept of divine inheritance, asserting that the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt are the rightful heirs to the earth as the ultimate *muttaqin*. It establishes a practical framework where Muslims retain ownership rights upon paying *kharaj* to the Imam, a system that persists until the reappearance of Al-Qa'im, who will consolidate land control while preserving the holdings of the Shia. This text highlights the unique Shia view of the Imam's temporal authority over land resources, linking spiritual piety with economic stewardship.
